The whole pipeline on one page

Two photos overlap. To join them you need to know which pixel in photo A is the same real-world point as which pixel in photo B. That is a three step recipe from the lecture: extract features, match features, align the images.

Your two photos

Real output · solved notebook · your two images

Everything in the blocks marked real output was produced by running the solved notebook on these two files, not drawn by hand.

Why use local features at all? The lecture lists four reasons: they are local (robust to occlusion and clutter), there are many of them (hundreds or thousands per image), they are distinctive, and they are efficient. Applications beyond stitching include 3D reconstruction, tracking, recognition and navigation.

Task 1Slides 10–43

Detection: where to look

Not every pixel is useful. A pixel in a blue sky matches a thousand other sky pixels. A useful keypoint is unusual, so that it has only one plausible partner in the other image. The slides ask for three properties: repeatability (found again in the other image), saliency (distinctive neighbourhood), and locality (small area, so occlusion does not break it).

The sliding window test

Take a small window and imagine shifting it. What happens to the pixels inside it?

Harris corner detector

Harris turns that sliding test into a number. For each pixel, look at the image derivatives Ix and Iy inside a window and build a 2×2 matrix from them:

M = Σ w(x,y) · [ Ix·Ix Ix·Iy ] [ Ix·Iy Iy·Iy ]

The eigenvalues λ1 and λ2 of M say how much the image changes along the two main gradient directions. If you rotate the corner, the eigenvalues stay the same, which is why Harris is rotation invariant (slide 27).

  • Both small: flat.
  • One large, one small: edge.
  • Both large: corner.

To avoid computing eigenvalues, the lecture uses a shortcut that only needs the determinant and trace:

f = det(M) − k · trace(M)² = λ1·λ2 − k·(λ1 + λ2)² k ≈ 0.04 to 0.06

Try it. Move the two sliders, or click the plot. The thresholds here are only for illustration; the notebook picks its own.

From response map to keypoints

The lecture shows three steps on a toy image. Compute f everywhere, keep pixels above a threshold, then keep only local maxima (non-maximum suppression) so each corner yields one point and not a cluster of neighbours.

Limit to rememberHarris is not scale invariant (slide 27). Zoom into a rounded corner and it looks like a straight edge inside the window. Your two images show the monument at different sizes, so this matters in Task 8.

Blob detection and scale

The fix for scale is to look at many sizes at once. The Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) is a circular filter that responds strongly to a blob of matching size. Run it at several σ values, and each blob gets a characteristic scale: the σ where the response peaks (slides 29–40). Interest points are local maxima in position and scale, so each is a triple (x, y, σ).

SIFT uses exactly this idea: it finds extrema of a difference-of-Gaussians stack. So for the SIFT half of the assignment you can let cv2.SIFT_create().detectAndCompute detect keypoints for you. For the patch half, the assignment tells you to use Harris or blob detection.

Task 2a, 2bSlides 44–54

Description: turning a neighbourhood into a vector

A keypoint is just a position. To compare keypoints across images you need a vector of numbers that summarises what is around each one. Two forces pull against each other (slide 47): invariance (the vector should not change when the image is rotated, scaled or brightened) and discriminability (the vector should be different for different places).

Option A: SIFT descriptor

  1. Take a 16×16 window around the keypoint.
  2. Compute the gradient direction and strength at every pixel. Drop weak gradients.
  3. Split the window into a 4×4 grid of cells.
  4. In each cell build a histogram of gradient directions with 8 bins.
  5. Concatenate: 16 cells × 8 bins = 128 numbers.

Rotation invariance comes from a detail in the slides: the histogram bins are shifted so the strongest orientation comes first, which makes the vector independent of how the patch is rotated. Scale invariance comes from the keypoint's scale σ, which sets the window size. SIFT copes with viewpoint changes of roughly 60° and a fair amount of lighting change (slide 53).

Option B: raw intensity patch

The simple option from the slides ("match square windows around the point"): cut an 11×11 window and read its pixels row by row into a vector of 121 numbers.

Practical tip, not from the slidesSubtract the patch mean and divide by its standard deviation before flattening. It costs one line and removes most of the brightness and contrast difference between the two photos. Also skip keypoints closer than 5 pixels to the border, otherwise the 11×11 window falls off the image.

This pair is the experiment the assignment is built around. SIFT carries a lot of invariance. The raw patch carries none. Task 8 asks you to measure the difference.

Tasks 3, 4, 5Slides 55–58

Matching: pairwise distances and putative matches

Compare every descriptor in image 1 with every descriptor in image 2 using Euclidean distance. That gives a table with one row per keypoint in image 1 and one column per keypoint in image 2.

d(a, b) = sqrt( Σ (a_i − b_i)² ) a, b are descriptors (128 or 121 long)

Choosing which matches to keep (Task 4)

"Putative" means plausible but unverified. The assignment accepts a fixed distance threshold or the top-N smallest distances, and asks you to explain your choice. The lecture adds a third strategy that is more robust: the ratio test.

Drag the thresholds on this made-up set of 14 matches (sorted by distance). Bars are the best-match distance. Matches must pass both limits.

What to write in the notebookState your rule and the reason. For example: "Keep matches whose nearest/second-nearest ratio is below 0.8, because it removes ambiguous matches without needing a distance scale that differs between SIFT and raw patches." If you use a fixed distance for one descriptor, say how you picked it, since the two descriptors live on very different numeric scales.

Visualising (Task 5)

Put the two images side by side in one canvas. Draw a line from each keypoint in the left image to its partner, using the right image's x-coordinate plus the left image's width as the offset. Good matches fan out as roughly parallel lines. Wrong ones cross at odd angles, as seen on slide 61.

Even after the ratio test, some wrong pairs survive. Removing them is the next job, and it needs geometry, not descriptors.

Task 6, 7 backgroundSlides 65–76, 94–110

Homography: the geometry behind the stitch

A ladder of transformations

A transformation maps points of one image onto the other. The slides climb from simple to general:

Homogeneous coordinates

A shift is x' = x + tx, which is not a matrix multiplication on (x, y) (slide 67). The trick: add a third coordinate, so (x, y) becomes (x, y, 1). Now shifts, rotations, scales and even perspective are all one 3×3 matrix multiply. To get back to pixels, divide by the third coordinate: (x, y, w) → (x/w, y/w).

The homography matrix

[ x' ] [ h00 h01 h02 ] [ x ] [ y' ] ~ [ h10 h11 h12 ] [ y ] then divide by the third component [ w' ] [ h20 h21 h22 ] [ 1 ]

The nine numbers are only defined up to scale, so there are 8 unknowns. Each point pair gives 2 equations (one for x', one for y'). Therefore 4 point pairs are the minimum to solve for H exactly. That is the number RANSAC will sample.

Solving for H from point pairs (the direct linear transform)

Multiply out the division and every pair gives two rows that are linear in the nine unknowns h. Stack 4 or more pairs into a matrix A and the problem becomes A·h = 0. Because h is only known up to scale, pick the unit-length h that makes A·h as small as possible. The slides' answer: the eigenvector of AᵀA with the smallest eigenvalue (equivalently, the last row of Vᵀ from the SVD of A).

Which OpenCV function whencv2.getPerspectiveTransform takes exactly 4 point pairs and returns the exact H. That is perfect for inside the RANSAC loop. For the final refit on all inliers you need least squares, either your own DLT with np.linalg.svd or cv2.findHomography(src, dst, 0) (method 0 means plain least squares, no RANSAC).

One more condition from the slides: a homography between two photos is exact only if the camera rotated about its optical centre, or the scene is flat or very far away (slides 100–116). Your photos are a handheld pan of a monument with trees in the foreground, so expect small misalignments where objects are close.

The bottom row is not (0, 0, 1). The small non-zero values in it (SIFT: about -0.0007 and -0.0001) are the perspective part, and they are what stretches the far side of the picture. The two matrices are similar but not identical: the patch one rests on far fewer matches.

Task 6Slides 76–93, 111

RANSAC: fitting through the noise

Least squares treats every match as truth. One wrong pair pulls the whole answer toward it (slides 77–79). RANSAC (RANdom SAmple Consensus) flips the logic: guess a model from a tiny random sample, then count how many other points agree. If a wrong point is in the sample, the model gets little support and is discarded.

Watch it on a line first

The lecture teaches RANSAC with line fitting because it is easy to see. Here the sample size is 2 points, the green band is the inlier threshold t, and the green points are the inliers of the current guess. Run a few iterations and notice how the best count only goes up.

The same loop for a homography

Slide 111 gives the recipe the notebook implements. Only two things change from the line version: a sample is 4 matches, and "distance to the model" is the reprojection error.

The numbers Task 6 asks for

Inlier count. The number of putative matches whose error is under ε for the final H.

Average squared reprojection error. Take a keypoint p from image 1, push it through H to get H·p (a predicted position in image 2), and measure how far that lands from the real matched point p'. Square that distance, and average over the inliers.

Parameters, in plain words

  • ε (inlier threshold): how far a point may land from its target and still count. 3 to 5 pixels is a common starting range for a 800 px wide image. Too tight rejects good matches, too loose accepts bad ones.
  • N (iterations): enough that at least one sample is all inliers. With inlier fraction r and sample size s, success probability p needs N ≥ log(1−p) / log(1−rˢ). For r = 0.5, s = 4, p = 0.99, that is about 72. For r = 0.2 it is about 2,880, which shows why slide 93 says RANSAC struggles with low inlier ratios.
  • Degenerate samples: if 3 of the 4 sampled points are on one line, H is unstable. Skip such samples or let the loop discard them via the inlier count.
Why this matters for Task 8Raw patches will produce more wrong putative matches, so the inlier ratio drops, and RANSAC may need many more iterations or fail outright. If the patch result is poor, say that and give the inlier count. A failed experiment that is explained earns more than a hidden one.

Notice that the inlier errors are small for both descriptors. A low error says the inliers agree with H, not that H is right for the whole scene, which is why the inlier count and spread must be read together with it.

RANSAC is random

Every RANSAC run draws different random samples. To see how much that matters, the whole step was repeated with 100 different seeds. SIFT found between 115 and 123 inliers and always gave a usable canvas (width 1633 to 2033 px). The patch descriptor found between 11 and 25 inliers, and its canvas width ranged from 800 to 273,771 px: in 24 of 100 runs the homography was unusable (a canvas of more than 40 million pixels). The pictures in this guide use the median usable run for each descriptor. The run saved in your notebook (SIFT 118 inliers, patch 19) is one more draw from the same spread.

Task 7Slides 59, 99–116

Panorama: warp, size the canvas, blend

Slide 100 gives the procedure: compute the transformation between the second image and the first, transform the second to overlap the first, and blend. The new problem is that the warped image can land at negative coordinates or beyond the first image's border, so the output canvas must be sized first.

Sizing the canvas

  1. Take the four corners of image 2 and push them through H. They give a quadrilateral in image 1's coordinates.
  2. Combine those four points with the four corners of image 1 and take the bounding box.
  3. If the box starts at negative coordinates, shift everything by (−min_x, −min_y) using a translation matrix T. Warp image 2 with T·H and place image 1 at offset (−min_x, −min_y).
  4. The canvas size is the box's width and height.

Why warping runs backwards

Pushing each source pixel forward leaves holes in the result. Instead, for every pixel in the output, use the inverse transform to find where it came from in the source (slide 112). That source location usually falls between pixels, so you interpolate from neighbours (nearest or bilinear). cv2.warpPerspective does all of this for you, pass it H and the canvas size.

Blending

The assignment allows two simple ways to fill the overlap. Both need a mask that says where each image has real pixels (a warped image has black borders that are not real black).

AverageWhere both masks are on, output = (a + b) / 2. Smooth transition in brightness, but any misalignment shows as ghosting.
Take oneWhere both masks are on, copy image 1 and ignore image 2. Sharp, no ghosts, but a visible seam if exposure differs.

Use floats while blending and convert to uint8 at the end, otherwise the sum of two 8-bit values wraps around. For Task 8, judge the panorama by looking at seams, ghosting along straight edges such as the colonnade, and the shape of the canvas.

Task 8 + conclusionSlides 47–53

Comparing SIFT with raw patches

Task 8 asks for four measurements per descriptor. Collect them in a small table in the notebook, then explain it using the invariance ideas from earlier.

MeasureWhat to reportWhat to expect (hypothesis to test)
Putative matchesCount after your threshold or ratio testPatches usually give many matches that are wrong, since raw pixels are not distinctive.
RANSAC inliersCount, and inliers ÷ putativeSIFT should have a clearly higher inlier ratio.
Reprojection errorMean squared error over inliersCompare carefully: a lower error with only 8 inliers is not better than a slightly higher one with 200.
Panorama qualityAlignment, seams, ghostingA bad H gives a warped, skewed or empty second image.

Why the difference should appear here

  • The monument looks larger in the right photo than in the left. A 11×11 patch covers a different physical area at each scale, so raw pixels no longer line up. SIFT's scale selection handles this.
  • The photos differ slightly in brightness and tone. SIFT's gradient histograms ignore most of that. Raw patches do not, unless you normalise them.
  • Harris is not scale invariant, so for the patch pipeline even the keypoints themselves may not repeat between the photos.
Conclusion templateSay what you measured, which descriptor won on each measure, and why, tying it back to invariance and discriminability (slide 47). Mention one limitation, such as parallax from the near trees or the assumption of a pure camera rotation.
